clean_claim:
I found no live credentials anywhere in this scope (high confidence). Every secret-shaped hit was checked in context and is a synthetic test fixture: example.invalid/user:secret URLs, a *-test-only Postgres password on 127.0.0.1, a BEGIN PRIVATE KEY header inside a castle test string, and a FlyV1 shape regex with a C-repeat fixture. There are no 0x40-hex wallet addresses, real JWTs, Stripe/AWS/GitHub/npm/Slack/HF tokens, Alchemy/Helius keys, phone numbers or street addresses. The only emails are git@github.com remotes, synthetic test URLs and one public vendor address. IPs are loopback or certificate OIDs. Fixtures with real-data shape (production-shape, handshake) self-declare synthetic and use repeated-digit machine IDs.

limits:
- **Reading coverage:** for the huge operator files I relied on targeted searches, not line-by-line reading: bin/deploy.sh (220 KB), bin/phase-b-refence-maintenance-contract.ts and -bridge.ts (about 500 KB each), their tests (about 500 KB), and the 4.7 MB production-shape fixture (structure dump and pattern scans only). I also searched, rather than read in full, the long test files and long creative scripts beyond their headers. That includes the joke and truth arrays in mindicraft-heartbeat.ts, telnet-truth.py, dark-continent.ts, greed-island.ts, nen-dojo.ts, solo-leveling.ts, the tax-*.ts files and hmrc-roast.ts. I sampled their content; prose-level relational or private content inside them that none of my patterns or name heuristics hit could be missed.
- **Names of private people:** my name check used capitalised First-Last pairs, CJK phrase listing and keywords. A private person referred to by first name only, a nickname or a handle without '@' could slip through.
- **Live vs synthetic identifiers:** that the Fly machine IDs and run IDs are real production values is my inference from context, not verified against Fly.
- **Copyright:** the third-party judgment on river.py is not legal advice. I did not check the Gospel content itself, which is outside this scope; only its release tooling is here.
- **Dependencies outside scope:** some fixes depend on files I was not asked to audit (api/tests/doctrine filenames, apps/docs RING-1.md, docs/*). Other repo files already carry the Supabase ref.
- **Network checks:** I made exactly two GETs (npm registry metadata; docs.agenttool.dev/RING-1.md) with a generic user agent and no identity.
- **Guard and checksum notes:** I did not run gitleaks or the project's own guard; the separate mechanical scan covers that. My regexes are a Python port of the guard's JS patterns, so small differences are possible. No downloaded tools were used, so there was nothing to checksum.
